title: Mississippi Senate: Scott Colom extends tight lead over Hyde-Smith as ballot deadlines hit
description: Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks with reporters at the OffBeat Records shop in Jackson, Mississippi, Nov. 6, 2026.Brandon Bell | Getty I
body: Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks with reporters at the OffBeat Records shop in Jackson, Mississippi, Nov. 6, 2026.Brandon Bell | Getty ImagesDemocratic nominee Scott Colom added slightly to his narrow lead over incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi Senate election as two key ballot deadlines hit Tuesday.Colom, a local district attorney, as of 4:30 p.m. ET, was ahead of Hyde-Smith by 2,607 votes, out of 953,547 votes counted, with an estimated 97% of the votes in, according to the Associated Press. That's a margin of just 0.27 percentage points.Independent candidate Ty Pinkins had 20,034 votes.Tuesday is the deadline for resolving affidavit or provisional ballots, which are cast by voters whose eligibility is disputed or unclear on Election Day. It is also the deadline for the receipt of mail-in absentee ballots that are postmarked by Election Day, Nov. 3.Mississippi is one of just two states whose Senate election has not been called. Alaska is the other.Democrats so far have flipped seven Senate seats held by Republicans going into the election. That gives Democrats a new majority in the Senate of at least 54 seats in the 100-member chamber come January.Alaska before Election Day was viewed as possibly key to the question of whether Republicans would retain their narrow majority in the Senate. Mississippi, which has not elected a Democratic senator since the segregationist John Stennis in 1982, was on few political analysts' radar as a possible pickup for Democrats. If Colom wins his race, he would be the first Black senator from Mississippi since the post-Civil War Reconstruction Era.In Alaska, Democratic nominee Mary Peltola is ahead by just 2,517 votes over incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, with 218,641 total votes counted, a margin of 1.1 percentage points. Peltola has 48.6% of the total vote. If neither she nor Sullivan gets more than 50% of the total vote, the race will go to a ranked-choice round, in which the two other candidates, Gerald Heikes and another candidate named Dan Sullivan, will be eliminated, and the second choices of voters who made them their first choice will be allocated between Peltola and the incumbent.

schema.headline: Mississippi Senate: Scott Colom extends tight lead over Hyde-Smith as ballot deadlines hit

title: Nvidia hires law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead Jensen Huang affair probe
description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks on stage during the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin, Germany, October 19, 2026.Lisi Niesner | ReutersNvidia's board
body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks on stage during the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin, Germany, October 19, 2026.Lisi Niesner | ReutersNvidia's board of directors said on Tuesday that it hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation of CEO Jensen Huang and whether company secrets or national security was compromised, after Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman who has been connected to Chinese intelligence."The independent members of the NVIDIA Board have retained former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a thorough and independent investigation as was announced on Sunday," the board said in a statement. Kim joined the firm last month, and he was previously the chief U.S. prosecutor in Manhattan, according to Law360. Nvidia has been thrust into turmoil since Huang's acknowledgement of the affair over the weekend. The chipmaker's stock dropped 6% on Tuesday after falling more than 4% on Monday, as investors worry that the investigation and scandal could result in the co-founder and CEO being forced out.Nvidia and the board are facing pressure from critics and politicians over what the company knew about sales of its restricted AI chips to Chinese companies.Over the past few weeks, The New York Times and Financial Times have reported that U.S. intelligence agencies surveilled an Asian technology executive, Alice Huang, who has been affiliated with Nvidia customer Megaspeed. These agencies have concluded that she is passing information to Beijing and is involved with Chinese intelligence, according to the reports.Huang has become the face of the AI industry, going by his first name "Jensen" to customers and rivals as Nvidia's technology is used to train nearly all major AI models. The chipmaker has become an essential source of financing for AI startups and Huang has met with presidents and CEOs around the world as Nvidia's public face. But Huang's actions have thrown the chipmaker into instability as he admitted to an affair with Alice Huang in an email to staff on Sunday. "My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang wrote in the message, while emphasizing that he is an American and supports U.S. national security.An Nvidia representative said at the time that Huang was committed to continuing as CEO of Nvidia without interruption.On Sunday, Nvidia's board said that it would investigate the allegations that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Nvidia's board also said on Sunday that it has no reason to believe either national security nor Nvidia secrets were compromised. This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates.

schema.headline: Nvidia hires law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead Jensen Huang affair probe

title: Anthropic opens Australian retail IPO offering as AI scrutiny intensifies
description: Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesAnthropic, the maker of AI chatbot Claude, opened its Australian retail initial public offering on Wednesday, g
body: Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesAnthropic, the maker of AI chatbot Claude, opened its Australian retail initial public offering on Wednesday, giving individual investors access to shares ahead of the company's planned Nasdaq listing.The offering opened at 10 a.m. Australian Eastern Daylight Time on Wednesday and is expected to close at 5 p.m. on Nov. 17, according to the timetable published by participating broker Stake.Anthropic is seeking to raise as much as $64.4 billion in its IPO, with a separate $26 billion private placement, bringing a combined total to as much as $90.4 billion. Shares are expected to be priced between $70 to $78 each. The Australian retail offering is expected to consist of newly issued Class A common shares under a prospectus to be lodged with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, Anthropic said on its website.Participating brokers include Commonwealth Bank of Australia's CommSec unit as lead broker, along with Bell Potter, LGT Wealth, Macquarie Group, Morgans, Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, Sharesies and Stake.Anthropic said the prospectus would be available on its IPO website once the Australian retail offering opens. Investors will need to review the document and apply through participating brokers under the terms of the offer.Australia is one of the small numbers of markets outside the U.S. where retail investors will be able to buy the company's shares directly, alongside Japan, Canada and parts of Europe. The San Francisco-based AI startup has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol "ANT." Anthropic said it does not plan to seek a listing on the Australian Securities Exchange.AI scrutiny growsThe offering comes as Australia moves to tighten oversight of AI companies after an OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to the medical statistics website of Medicare,  the country's universal health insurance program.Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Tuesday that the government would introduce mandatory reporting for certain AI-related incidents and establish an AI safety regulator with powers to enforce penalties. "The law needs to get ahead of, and in some cases, make sure that it catches up with what is a very fast-changing world," Albanese told Reuters.The government is also considering changes to criminal law for cases involving serious misconduct.The country has also ruled out a copyright-law exemption that would allow AI companies to train models on Australian content without licensing it. Open AI and Anthropic told Australian parliament last month that they would support mandatory reporting of data breaches involving their AI agents, acknowledging that disclosure is currently voluntary.

schema.headline: Anthropic opens Australian retail IPO offering as AI scrutiny intensifies

title: American soldier arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia
description: An American flag is displayed on a U.S. Army uniform at Marine Corps Air Station Miramar on September 25, 2026 in San Diego, CA.Kevin Carter | Getty I
body: An American flag is displayed on a U.S. Army uniform at Marine Corps Air Station Miramar on September 25, 2026 in San Diego, CA.Kevin Carter | Getty ImagesA senior soldier in the U.S. Army has been arrested in the U.K. on suspicion of spying for Russia, London's Metropolitan Police said on Tuesday evening. The unnamed 41-year-old man was arrested near Gloucester, a city in western England, on Tuesday as part of an investigation by the U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing. British police worked with U.S. authorities, including the military and the FBI, in their investigations.A senior NATO military official confirmed on Tuesday that the American service member was assigned to the military alliance's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC). ARRC, headquartered in the English county of Gloucestershire, is a  3-star NATO headquarters with more than 400 permanent staff from more than 20 nations ready to deploy land forces where they are needed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday that Moscow had "absolutely nothing to do with" the case in the U.K.The individual at the center of the case, detained in London, is suspected of committing offenses under Sections 1 and 3 of the U.K.'s National Security Act. Section 1 offenses relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while Section 3 involves assisting a foreign intelligence service. The maximum penalty is life imprisonment for a Section 1 offense and 14 years' imprisonment for a Section 3 offense. A fine may also be imposed for either offense.Police officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire, the Metropolitan Police added.U.S. mediates Russia-Ukraine talksThe arrest comes as Washington is seeking to broker an end to Russia's war in Ukraine. U.S.-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials began in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, the first such meeting since February, while Kyiv and its European allies continue to press for credible security guarantees as part of any settlement.President Donald Trump, a longstanding critic of NATO and its members' defense budgets, said on Monday that there appeared to be a growing willingness on both sides to end the almost five-year war. Russia has long threatened retaliatory action against an expansion of NATO's eastern flank and has previously demanded guarantees that Ukraine will never be allowed to join the alliance. Finland and Sweden became NATO's newest members in 2023 and 2024, respectively. Since Russia and Ukraine have been at war, Russian activity has also been reported deeper into European and NATO territory, with regional authorities investigating whether Moscow could be involved in some of the recent disarray seen across the continent. FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement on Tuesday evening that the allegations against a U.S. serviceman were "of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies.""I want to send a clear message – this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners," he said. The alleged conduct of a senior solider, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.Sean StinchonCommanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence CommandSean Stinchon, the commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, said in a statement that "the alleged conduct of a senior solider, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent."Authorities said Tuesday that the investigation is not related to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations. On Oct. 27, British prosecutors said they had charged a man with assisting a foreign intelligence service over an incident at a military base used by the U.S. for strikes on Iran. The base in question, RAF Fairford, is in Gloucestershire, around 30 miles from ARRC's headquarters at Imjin Barracks.

schema.headline: American soldier arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia

title: Hegseth impeachment effort torpedoed in House
description: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth gestures as he speaks during a news conference at the Pentagon on November 10, 2026 in Arlington, Virginia. U.S.Ch
body: U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth gestures as he speaks during a news conference at the Pentagon on November 10, 2026 in Arlington, Virginia. U.S.Chip Somodevilla | Getty ImagesThe House of Representatives effectively torpedoed an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth with a procedural vote on Tuesday evening.The House, by a 211-204 margin, approved a measure that will refer the impeachment resolution to a committee.That will leave little, if any, time for the committee and full House to act on it before Democrats take over the chamber and the Senate with a new majority in early January. House Republican leadership had sought to kill the effort at impeachment, which was initiated Monday by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky.The vote came a week after the midterm elections, where Democrats trounced Republicans in the first congressional election since the Iran war broke out in February.Hegseth had faced eight articles of impeachment.Massie accused Hegseth of waging war in contravention of Congress, carrying out extrajudicial killings tied to boat strikes in the Caribbean against purported drug smugglers and suppressing free speech by targeting Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a military veteran.Massie is a libertarian who lost his Republican primary in May after clashing with President Donald Trump. The Kentucky Republican led a bill last year to compel the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Shortly after the vote, Trump said: "Democrats' attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED!" "Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favor of Pete," the president said, declaring what he said was an "EXONERATION" of Hegseth. A Republican forced the vote on Hegseth's impeachment. All Democrats voted against referring the measure to committee. Defense Department spokesperson Jacob Bliss said earlier in the day that Hegseth "carried out direct, lawful orders from the President to secure the nation." The impeachment effort notably focused on Hegseth, not Trump, who is responsible for launching the various military operations referred to in the articles. Hegseth, at a press conference at the Pentagon earlier Tuesday, railed against Massie and defended his leadership in the Iran war and other military operations."What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it's not accountability. It's a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment," Hegseth said Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) discusses articles of impeachment he introduced against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the U.S. Capitol Building on November 09, 2026 in Washington, D.C.Finn Gomez | Getty Images"It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it," Hegseth said. "It puts a target on the backs of American warriors by signaling that Congress will undermine their missions in real time."This is not patriotism. This is sabotage."Trump, in a Truth Social post on Tuesday, said  Hegseth "gets an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!"Trump said Monday that he would stand by Hegseth even if the House impeached him. The president was impeached by the House two times during his first White House term. The Senate acquitted him in both cases.Republicans hold a slim 218-214 majority in the House.Some Republicans, notably including Vice President JD Vance, have directly blamed their midterm losses on the Iran war, which continues to see intermittent fighting amid an uneasy stalemate.Neither of the two Cabinet secretaries impeached by the House has ever been removed by the Senate after a trial in that chamber.

schema.headline: Hegseth impeachment effort torpedoed in House

title: House Oversight calls on DOJ to interview key Epstein witnesses, says govt. ‘failed’ survivors
description: Epstein abuse survivor Lisa Phillips speaks during a news conference with lawmakers on the Epstein Files Transparency Act outside the U.S. Capitol on
body: Epstein abuse survivor Lisa Phillips speaks during a news conference with lawmakers on the Epstein Files Transparency Act outside the U.S. Capitol on November 18, 2025 in Washington, DC. Heather Diehl | Getty ImagesThe House Oversight and Government Reform Committee on Tuesday released a sharply critical report on the federal government's handling of investigations into Jeffrey Epstein and his accomplice, Ghislaine Maxwell."The federal government has failed the survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell's horrific crimes for decades," Oversight Chair Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., said in a statement.The report called for the Justice Department to interview or reinterview "key witnesses" with information about Epstein's sex trafficking of young women and girls, "further investigate allegations of criminal activity involving Epstein's associates, and provide survivors with unredacted access to their records."The report also urged Congress to pass legislation sponsored by Comer that would allow survivors of sexual abuse to speak freely about it, even if they had signed confidentiality agreements.In addition to criticizing the federal government, the committee blasted various financial institutions for their roles in dealing with Epstein, who killed himself in August 2019 in jail after being arrested on child sex trafficking charges."U.S. and foreign government authorities failed to identify indicators of human trafficking and immigration fraud," the committee said. "Institutions such as American Express enabled this activity, with company agents allowing Epstein to use fraudulent decoy flights and refundable or dummy itineraries to transport foreign women across borders directly to his residences."House Oversight Committee chairman Representative James Comer, Republican from Kentucky, speaks to the press as Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates participates in a closed-door interview with the House Oversight Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, on June 10, 2026. Kent Nishimura | Afp | Getty Images"Financial institutions possessed substantial information about Epstein's criminal history and repeatedly identified transactions and activities presenting heightened compliance risks," the committee said. "Yet they failed to adequately address those risks, in some cases reporting them years later after Epstein's 2019 arrest, due to Epstein's personal connections, wealth, and influence."The committee called on the Treasury Department and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network to review whether banks and other financial institutions are meeting their obligations to report activity that could point to money laundering and human trafficking.The committee has been investigating Epstein, Maxwell and their connections since last year.

schema.headline: House Oversight calls on DOJ to interview key Epstein witnesses, says govt. ‘failed’ survivors

title: White House vows to press ahead with tariffs despite midterm backlash over rising prices
description: Business leaders participate in a panel discussion at the B20 summit, hosted by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in Washington, D.C., Nov. 10, 2026.Luke F
body: Business leaders participate in a panel discussion at the B20 summit, hosted by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in Washington, D.C., Nov. 10, 2026.Luke Fountain | CNBCOne week after voters punished Republicans over rising prices in the midterm elections, President Donald Trump's White House signaled it would stay the course on tariffs, even as his former top economic advisor warned that Americans are footing the bill.Jim Goyer, Trump's director of White House Office of Public Liaison, defended tariffs as a tool to rebuild U.S. manufacturing, secure supply chains and protect national security during an address Tuesday at the B20 summit, a gathering of global business leaders in Washington hosted by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce."And we are just getting started," Goyer said. "Our ambition is to continue this pace for the remainder of the president's term in office."But Gary Cohn, who served as Trump's chief economic advisor during his first administration, offered a sharply different assessment during an onstage interview later Tuesday."Tariffs are a consumption tax on the U.S. consumer," Cohn said, arguing that the duties are raising prices and forcing Americans to reconsider purchases.The divide exposed a growing dilemma for Trump. His trade agenda is reshaping global commerce – and driving up costs for voters. Companies are adapting to the chaos, but the old trading system isn't coming back."President Trump has disrupted that system in a way that we're not likely to return to," Kevin Brady, a former Republican congressman who helped lead the B20 summit,  said during a discussion with U.S. Chamber CEO Suzanne Clark.The political backlash was evident in the Nov. 3 election. Roughly two-thirds of voters said Trump's policies contributed to inflation, according to the CNBC Voter Poll. Nearly nine in 10 said the cost of living was a major or crucial factor in their vote.A separate Reuters/Ipsos poll released Tuesday found 62% of Americans supported repealing Trump's tariffs, while just 21% approved of his handling of the cost of living."Last week, American voters sent a clear message about the cost of living and their economic security," Clark said in her keynote address. The pressure intensified Tuesday as new government data showed consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, exceeding economists' expectations. Annual inflation reached 3.7% in September, the latest available year-over-year figure and well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target.Tariffs are not the only factor driving higher prices. The war with Iran has pushed energy costs sharply higher, while housing, healthcare and other household expenses continue to strain consumers.But research has found Trump's import duties have added to those pressures. A Federal Reserve Bank of New York study estimated that about 26% of tariff increases were passed through to consumer prices, with some effects taking nine to 12 months to work through supply chains.Cohn, now vice chairman of IBM, argued that while tariffs generate revenue for the U.S., those gains come at consumers' expense."You're looking at one side of the equation. You're looking at the credit side of the balance sheet," Cohn said, describing how he would respond to Trump's defense of tariff revenue. "There's the debit side of the balance sheet, which is every hardworking American who happened to pay the tariff through some product that they bought."Still, Cohn saw room for a bipartisan trade deal. He suggested Trump and the incoming Democratic Congress could make protections against China and unfair trade practices permanent while rolling back tariffs on Canada, leaving less for future presidents to undo.For businesses, the shift is already underway. UPS CEO Carol Tomé said customers are moving production and sourcing closer to home as global supply chains become more regional."Supply chains are diversifying. Supply chains are regionalizing," Tomé said during a panel discussion moderated by CNBC's Morgan Brennan.Separately, UPS is opening a new $80 million-plus air hub in the Philippines in October to expand its Asian network and improve connections across more than 1,100 global trade lanes.Other executives, like Jim Fitterling, executive chairman of chemicals giant Dow, defended Trump's tariffs despite their costs. Fitterling acknowledged they can drive up prices but argued they are necessary to combat unfair competition and protect U.S. manufacturing.Democrats plan to challenge Trump's tariffs when they take control of Congress in January, but his veto power and broad trade authority could make them difficult to overturn.

schema.headline: White House vows to press ahead with tariffs despite midterm backlash over rising prices

title: Investors pivot to defensive stocks as markets enter a ‘state of alert’
description: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Sept. 16, 2026.Jeenah Moon | ReutersMarkets are in a "state of alert," according to analysts
body: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Sept. 16, 2026.Jeenah Moon | ReutersMarkets are in a "state of alert," according to analysts monitoring a pivot from riskier tech sector bets into defensive stocks. Technology stocks — a key driver of rallies in recent years — have been notably volatile in 2026. Concerns about artificial intelligence — particularly when it comes to capital expenditure, cash flow, debt and circular financing — have sparked multiple bouts of volatility this year.The Democrats' sweep of Congress in the U.S. midterm elections amplified pressure on the sector last week. Wall Street's tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index is up by around 8.7% since the start of the year as of Nov. 9 close, but gave up some of its year-to-date gains in October when it shed 5.3% over the course of the month. The index — home to Big Tech names including Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet and Apple — has staged a recovery in recent days, but remains in the red for November and is down 0.7% for the month so far after dipping into correction territory last week. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNasdaq Composite's performance over the past monthThe Nasdaq isn't the only tech-focused index to have seen big losses over the past month. South Korea's Kospi index, which is heavily exposed to the semiconductor sector, lost 16.2% in October and is down more than 8% month-to-date. The MSCI World Information Technology index lost 7% in October, and has shed a further 4.6% so far this month. MSCI's U.S.-only IT index is down 11.5% since October. At the same time, stocks in defensive sectors have seen broad gains. MSCI's indexes encompassing the consumer staples, healthcare and utilities sectors — widely seen as more stable assets in the equity market during times of volatility or uncertainty — have all risen significantly over the last month. In a note on Monday, Alastair Pinder, HSBC's head emerging markets and global equity strategist, said recent moves in stock markets had been "vicious, and in our view, overdone.""The market is already pricing greater execution risk and capex delays," he said, referring to the development of artificial intelligence. "With US semiconductors trading on a 12-month forward PE of 13.5x after a 45% de-rating since June, how much more pain is there to price?"He added that fundamentals broadly appear healthy. "The rotation into defensives looks extreme," he said. "Walmart trades on 40x forward earnings, near a record high, while Nvidia trades on 13x, near a record low."Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, described equity markets as being "in a state of alert, judging by how investors are rotating their sector exposures.""Such movement matters, and can help stock pickers with their selections, bearing in mind the old adage that 'a bad stock in a good sector will outperform a good stock in a bad sector,'" he said in a note on Monday. AJ Bell's analysis of 11 so-called "super-sectors" in the S&P Global 1200 shows that, in the second half of 2026 so far, healthcare and consumer staples stocks have been the best performers after energy — a major beneficiary of surging oil prices in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war. The IT sector, the data shows, has gone from being the best-performing sector in the first half of the year on a 28.4% rise, to the worst performer in the second half after tumbling more than 11%.  "Information Technology has gone from penthouse to outhouse and slumped from being the best performer to the worst," Mould said. "Energy has been resilient as have Consumer Staples and Healthcare, while Industrials have been noticeably weak. These trends could reflect nagging worries over the economic outlook for next year, as well as worries over whether air is leaking out of an AI 'bubble.'"

schema.headline: Investors pivot to defensive stocks as markets enter a ‘state of alert’

title: Nvidia shares rebound 5% as Huang faces scrutiny ahead of earnings
description: Nvidia's stock rose premarket on Wednesday, after falling for two days amid the scandal that has rocked the world's most valuable tech company.Shares
body: Nvidia's stock rose premarket on Wednesday, after falling for two days amid the scandal that has rocked the world's most valuable tech company.Shares had closed down 5.47% on Tuesday as more details were revealed about the impact of CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy. They fell 4.3% Monday.Shares were 5.3% higher in premarket trading as of 5:47 a.m. ET.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNvidia shares over the past five days.On Tuesday, Nvidia announced it had hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether company secrets or national security were compromised.Huang tried to project "business as usual" as he returned to the office on Monday, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. The CEO was also in the office on Tuesday, conducting meetings, ahead of the company's quarterly earnings on Nov. 17.Investors are assessing whether the matter will have damaging spillover effects on the business.In a Tuesday note, Bank of America said it saw three scenarios with differing investment outcomes. In one scenario, the impact is contained with leadership continuity, and in another, prolonged uncertainty pressures valuation before earnings. watch nowIn the final scenario, the impact is escalated, with "adverse findings, leadership disruption or tighter restrictions requiring earnings reassessment," BofA research analyst Vivek Arya said in the note.Zacks' Chief Equity Strategist John Blank said the selloff reflected two concerns: that the U.S. might impose further restrictions in the wake of the affair and that further problems might arise as the news develops. "What else has Jensen done?" he said."It's not good for Nvidia. It's not good for Jensen Huang. It's certainly not good for the AI trade," Blank told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday.Morgan Stanley on Wednesday removed Nvidia as a top pick after shares dropped more than 25% since it was named on the list on Oct. 2. Huang's leadership is "crucial" to the company's strategic direction, analysts said in a Wednesday note.— CNBC's Michael Bloom helped contribute to this report.

schema.headline: Nvidia shares rebound 5% as Huang faces scrutiny ahead of earnings

title: Bessent reportedly moved to military base over Iranian threats on his life
description: U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent speaks during a press conference in St. Cloud, Minn. on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Leila Navidi | Star Tribun
body: U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent speaks during a press conference in St. Cloud, Minn. on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Leila Navidi | Star Tribune | Getty ImagesU.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was reportedly moved from his Washington, D.C., home to a military base due to Iranian threats on his life.The New York Times, citing officials familiar with the matter, said that U.S. officials had concluded Iranian plotting against current and former American officials had reached a more advanced stage. Separately, Reuters reported that the severity of the threats against Bessent was not immediately clear. Bessent has led "Operation Economic Outcast," a Treasury campaign launched in August to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and other financial measures, in addition to the U.S. military actions.The Times reported that Bessent's role in that campaign has made him one of the Trump administration officials Iran most wanted to target. The move comes as the Department of Justice Department said late Tuesday that three Iranian nationals had been indicted on terrorism-related charges. The department said the three were allegedly involved in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States.The alleged plots included a September 2026 attack targeting RAF Fairford in the U.K., where U.S. military personnel were stationed."Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government," Attorney General Todd Blanche said.Earlier in October, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Iran was involved in the incident at RAF Fairford that led to the arrest of five men on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences.Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi then rejected the allegation, writing on X that Burnham was "barking up the wrong tree."RAF Fairford, in Gloucestershire, is a key U.S. Air Force operating location in Europe and has supported deployments of American strategic bombers and other aircrafts.Stalled negotiations Separately, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly said military action against Iran may not be necessary if economic sanctions and Washington's naval blockade are working.On Monday, President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that "Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, and others, would prefer the status quo, in other words, a continuation of the Greatest Naval Blockade in History.""We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict," Trump added.Asked Tuesday why he would not simply declare an end to the Iran war, Trump said he wanted to ensure U.S. allies in the region were "not hurt" and that there was a "long term solution.However, Iranian officials have denied that negotiations are underway. Security chief Mohsen Rezaei said claims that talks were continuing were aimed at "easing economic pressures and reducing oil prices."Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude prices edged higher during Wednesday's Asia trading session, at about $92 and $86 per barrel, respectively.

schema.headline: Bessent reportedly moved to military base over Iranian threats on his life

title: How Democrats could snarl Trump administration stakes in private-sector companies
description: President Donald Trump speaks in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on Nov. 9, 2026 in Washington, D.C.Chip Somodevilla | Getty
body: President Donald Trump speaks in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on Nov. 9, 2026 in Washington, D.C.Chip Somodevilla | Getty ImagesWith Republicans in charge of the White House and Congress, President Donald Trump has embedded the federal government in private-sector companies' affairs in unprecedented ways. That could change once Trump's Democratic adversaries take over the House and Senate following the blue-wave midterm.Democrats, planning to root out alleged corruption involving Trump, his family and their business associates, have signaled they will closely scrutinize companies that have curried the president's favor. Their investigations may extend to Intel and the dozens of other companies that have clinched equity stakes with the government during Trump's second term. Democratic lawmakers in July asked law firm Skadden Arps for details about its involvement in the Intel deal.The dynamic could affect how Trump approaches relationships with private-sector companies, after spending two years involving the government in their affairs through stock agreements or, in the case of U.S. Steel, acquiring a "golden share" when the company was acquired by Nippon Steel.The golden share, which allows a holder to outvote other shareholders, was negotiated as part of the June 2025 deal. The highly unusual arrangement gives Trump veto power over several key areas of the steelmaker's business, including those related to employee salaries, capital investment and even the company name. In a unique twist, the company's amended charter specifies that after Trump leaves office, the veto power passes not to his successor, but to the Treasury and Commerce Departments as representatives of the U.S. government.U.S. Steel CEO David Burritt is scheduled to speak Wednesday with CNBC's Megan Cassella about what's next for U.S. industry at the B20 summit hosted by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.The U.S. Steel intervention turned out to be just the beginning of the U.S. government taking stakes in companies, a highly unusual move stateside. A month after acquiring the golden share, the Trump administration agreed to a $400 million stock deal with rare-earths company MP Materials. The month after that, Trump announced the U.S. would take a 10% stake in chipmaker Intel.By January, one year into Trump's second term as president, the administration had established some form of equity position in 14 companies, according to the CATO Institute's tracker. That number skyrocketed to 41 by November, including nine such announcements in May alone, the tracker shows. The holdings include both publicly traded and privately held companies, and CATO tracks deals that are closed as well as others that have been made public but are still being negotiated.Following Republicans' decisive defeat in the Nov. 3 midterm election, the federal government has not revealed any new stock positions. But Trump, entering lame-duck status and on the verge of losing political power over Congress, could keep trying to steer his government to forge more equity deals with companies, said Indiana University associate professor Sarah Bauerle Danzman, who researches the intersection of national security and investment policy."He might feel he has less to lose," Bauerle Danzman, who is also a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told CNBC.White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC in a statement, "Through voluntary equity investments in willing companies, the Trump Administration has partnered with the private sector to rebuild America's industrial base and bring critical production back home.""Moving forward, the President is willing to work with anyone to advance solutions that strengthen our economy and put more money back in the pockets of American workers," Middleton said.But Trump's so-far unimpeded efforts may face sudden resistance once Democrats take majority control of the House and Senate in January.Democratic lawmakers are openly gearing up to score wins against Trump and his associates as they vow to crack down on alleged rampant government corruption. Those probes are expected to center on tech giants like Apple, Meta Platforms and Elon Musk's companies, whose executives have spent millions cozying up to the administration. Democrats are also poised to dig into potential conflicts related to the bevy of critical-minerals deals Trump has struck. Lawmakers of both parties are also looking at Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the close Trump ally engulfed in scandal after admitting an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy.The administration's equity interventions could become a target in that mission, said Bauerle Danzman, predicting that Democrats might seek to boost oversight efforts even if they don't try to cancel the existing stock arrangements.The next Congress could try to ensure the government is taking stakes that are "forwarding genuine national security priorities" and that do not provide "special favors to political and family connections," she said."The story there is more about kind of tying these issues to ones of accountability and anti-corruption, as opposed to necessarily cost," Bauerle Danzman said.It's also not clear how strongly Republicans would try to defend Trump's golden share or his government's equity stakes should they become a Democratic target. Conservatives traditionally espouse free markets and denounce excessive government meddling in the private sector. Republicans, including Trump, spent much of the midterm campaign warning that Democrats aim to destroy the U.S. capitalist system and impose economy-killing big-government socialism.Some Republicans have criticized the Trump administration's corporate interventions, but the moves have received little pushback from the president's party overall.But in the wake of a crushing electoral defeat, some Republicans "might feel emboldened and actually join with the Democrats" in trying to clamp down on Trump, Bauerle Danzman said.

schema.headline: How Democrats could snarl Trump administration stakes in private-sector companies

title: Nissan CEO breaks down how it plans to fight back against Chinese companies, after second outlook cut in months
description: watch nowNissan Motor plans to expand exports of vehicles developed in China to help compete against Chinese rivals globally, CEO Ivan Espinosa told C
body: watch nowNissan Motor plans to expand exports of vehicles developed in China to help compete against Chinese rivals globally, CEO Ivan Espinosa told CNBC on Wednesday.The export push comes as intensifying competition in the world's largest auto market forced the company to cut its annual sales forecast for a second time in months.Espinosa said Nissan would rapidly increase its exports of China-developed vehicles from two models to five, targeting 12 regional market clusters in the "very near term."The Japanese automaker is responding to intensifying competition in China by developing vehicles specifically for Chinese consumers, using local technology, lower costs and faster development processes, he said."We can defend ourselves from these very aggressive players by using exactly the same elements that they have: speed, cost, and good technology," he told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe." China headwindsNissan faces weakening demand and an accelerating shift toward electric vehicles in China, even as its restructuring efforts show progress in the U.S. and Japan.On Wednesday, Nissan cut its global sales outlook for the fiscal year ending March 2027 to between 2.97 million and 3 million vehicles, down from 3.15 million previously. It maintained its full-year operating profit and net cash guidance.In China, "weaker demand, a faster-than-anticipated shift to [new energy vehicles] and intensifying competition are putting greater pressure on sales than initially anticipated," the company said in a statement.In August, Nissan revised its full-year sales volume outlook from 3.3 million units to 3.15 million units.In October, shares of peer Volvo Cars crashed after it reported a swing to operating loss, citing tough market conditions in China and the U.S. CEO Håkan Samuelsson told CNBC at the time that it needed a new strategy in China, with regionally adapted cars."It's really a lot about the Chinese market, of course, where the change has come faster than we thought, and really now we can see that selling global cars developed in Europe and China will not work, and then this is affecting all the Western players in China," Samuelsson said.watch nowOn Wednesday, Nissan also reported a 96% drop in second-quarter operating profit to 2.1 billion yen ($13 million), significantly below analyst expectations of 54.9 billion yen, according to FactSet. The drop in profits was due to no longer having the benefit of lower U.S. emissions-related expenses that boosted profits a year ago, the company said.Net revenue grew 8.2% to 3.1 trillion yen in the quarter, largely in line with consensus.The quarterly results came after the Tokyo market closed. Shares are down 29% year-to-date.Espinosa, who has led the company since April 2025, also emphasised progress on a turnaround plan to reduce its global manufacturing footprint and cut its workforce by 15%. About 18 months into the plan, the company has achieved 365 billion yen in savings, Espinosa said.

schema.headline: Nissan CEO breaks down how it plans to fight back against Chinese companies, after second outlook cut in months

title: Rep. Jim Jordan, Sen. John Thune elected GOP leaders in Congress
description: Rep. Jim Jordan (C), R-Ohio, walks to a meeting with House Republicans, where they will elect their party's leadership for the 120th Congress, at the
body: Rep. Jim Jordan (C), R-Ohio, walks to a meeting with House Republicans, where they will elect their party's leadership for the 120th Congress, at the US Capitol in Washington, D.C., Nov. 10, 2026.Jim Watson | Afp | Getty ImagesRepublican lawmakers on Tuesday picked Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio and Sen. John Thune of South Dakota to serve as their respective House and Senate minority leaders in the next Congress.Jordan, the House Judiciary Committee chairman, was elected in a 106-73 vote, sources told MS NOW on condition of anonymity to discuss the private meeting. He beat Rep. Steve Scalise, R-La., the current House majority leader.A two-decade House veteran and committed supporter of President Donald Trump, Jordan will take on the leadership role just as Republicans relinquish power, following blowout Democratic victories in last week's midterm election.House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced the day after Election Day that he would not run for minority leader in the 120th Congress.Thune, in a statement, said he "appreciated the opportunity to have an open, honest, and transparent conversation with my colleagues today, and I am honored to have their continued trust and support to lead the Senate Republican Conference in the 120th Congress."Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., arrives for the Senate Republican leadership elections in the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday, November 10, 2026. Tom Williams | Cq-roll Call, Inc. | Getty Images"I'm proud of what this Republican team has accomplished together, and we remain united in our commitment to advancing conservative priorities, working with President Trump and our colleagues in the House, and holding the line against Democrats' efforts to enact their far-left, liberal agenda," Thune said in the statement."We have important work ahead of us, and I look forward to serving alongside my colleagues on behalf of the American people," he said.

schema.headline: Rep. Jim Jordan, Sen. John Thune elected GOP leaders in Congress

title: Fossil CEO says turnaround is ahead of plan as sales return to growth
description: People walk past the Fossil store at the Woodbury Common Premium Outlets shopping mall in Central Valley, New York, Nov. 17, 2019.Gary Hershorn | Corb
body: People walk past the Fossil store at the Woodbury Common Premium Outlets shopping mall in Central Valley, New York, Nov. 17, 2019.Gary Hershorn | Corbis News | Getty ImagesFossil Group posted quarterly results on Tuesday that could point to early signs of a turnaround for the legacy watchmaker. The company, which has struggled to compete with new gadgets in the years since its sales and stock price peaked in the 2010s, has been quietly undertaking a comeback strategy under CEO Franco Fogliato. The company's fiscal third-quarter earnings indicate the strategy is beginning to bear fruit.The company said Tuesday that it returned to profitability in the third quarter, posting operating income of $25.3 million, compared with an operating loss of $21.7 million last year. It also returned to sales growth, with net sales up 0.4% to $271.2 million. The company last reported a year-over-year sales increase in the first fiscal quarter of 2022. "We're excited about improving dramatically the profitability of the company through a very strong and disciplined management of full-price sales as well as cost management," Fogliato told CNBC in an exclusive interview.For the quarter ended Oct. 3, Fossil reported net income of $11.7 million, or 19 cents per share, compared with a net loss of $39.9 million, or 76 cents per share, the year prior. The company also said its operating expenses fell 11.1% to $137 million. The company last posted quarterly net income in the third fiscal quarter of 2022.With the signs of growth, the retailer also raised its full-year outlook, guiding for full-year net sales of between $980 million and $990 million, which would mark a slight decline from just over $1 billion in net sales in the prior year. That compares with a previous expectation of net sales falling between 3% and 5%. Fossil also said it's expecting positive free cash flow by the end of the year. Fogliato said Fossil had previously not expected sales growth for another year and a half.The stronger quarter comes after the company saw slumping sales and financial losses over the past few years. It struggled with the rise of smartwatches, mounting debt and the decline in mall foot traffic.Fossil stock has lost the vast majority of its value since the early-to-mid 2010s, and despite a recent surge, was trading under $8 a share on Tuesday. To rightsize the business, Fogliato, who joined Fossil in 2024, said he focused on closing stores, moving away from promotions to full-price sales, improving marketing and broadening Fossil's product range. That meant shrinking the business to a sustainable baseline before trying to grow it.The company saw a 5.9% decrease in direct-to-consumer sales for its third quarter, which Fogliato attributed to the company's "aggressive" downsizing."We simplified a lot of the business doing this," Fogliato said, adding that customers responded well when the company moved away from markdowns. "People tell me they are excited about what they are seeing in the marketplace now."Fossil added that its key growth engine for the quarter was Asia, where net sales grew 15.1%. Fogliato said much of that growth was led by the India market.At the same time, growing internationally is only part of the watchmaker's strategy as it tries to improve its performance in its home country."Priority number one is to grow our home market, and we're doing that," he said. "As retail is settling into a smaller, more profitable base, ready to grow again, we're entering 2027 with plenty of opportunities." Fogliato said one key to growth was not trying to keep up with the smartwatch trend. While trying to make gains in the smartwatch space initially hampered Fossil's performance, it's now investing in analog watches again. Smartwatch sales came in under $1 million for the quarter, but sales for traditional watches — which make up around 86% of Fossil's sales — grew 6.4%. "Fossil is literally having a comeback, a strong comeback, a momentum, and we can see this," Fogliato said. "And it comes not only through the numbers — it comes with the excitement we see in the stores, and we think we're just at the beginning. We have so much work to do."

schema.headline: Fossil CEO says turnaround is ahead of plan as sales return to growth

title: How much you can make in 2027 and still pay 0% capital gains tax
description: Fg Trade Latin | E+ | Getty ImagesThe IRS has released the capital gains tax brackets for 2027, which include a six-figure earnings limit for the 0% r
body: Fg Trade Latin | E+ | Getty ImagesThe IRS has released the capital gains tax brackets for 2027, which include a six-figure earnings limit for the 0% rate for married couples. If you're eager to sell profitable brokerage account investments, higher income thresholds for the 0% rate could help reduce your tax bill, experts say. "The 0% capital gains bracket is easily one of the most overlooked strategies for tax-free income," said Stephen Maggard, a certified financial planner with Abacus Planning Group in Columbia, South Carolina.But it's important to know how the tax brackets work and the possible trade-offs before selling investments.   Despite recent stock market volatility, many investors have portfolio gains after years of market growth. As of market close Nov. 9,  the S&P 500 was up about 10% year-to-date. The index also returned more than 16% in 2025, and over 23% in 2024.If you're planning to leverage the 0% capital gains bracket in 2027 to sell or rebalance brokerage account assets, here are some key things to know.    How the 0% capital gains brackets workThe capital gains brackets — with rates of 0%, 15% or 20% — apply to assets owned for more than one year, known as long-term capital gains. By contrast, investments held for one year or less are short-term gains, subject to regular income tax rates. Your rate depends on taxable income, which you calculate by subtracting the greater of the standard or itemized deductions from your adjusted gross income, or AGI. Taxable income also includes any gains from investments that year. The standard deduction will rise to $16,600 for single taxpayers and $33,200 for married couples in 2027.For example, let's say a married couple's AGI is $130,000 for 2027, including capital gains. After subtracting the $33,200 standard deduction, their taxable income would be $96,800, which falls below the 0% threshold.However, taxable income should include mutual fund distributions, which can "dramatically alter year-end planning projections" and increase taxable income, according to CFP Jim Guarino, managing director at Baker Newman Noyes in Woburn, Massachusetts. He is also a certified public accountant.If your federal taxable income is above the 0% threshold, you'll pay 15% on the portion of investment gains that exceed the 0% limit, up to that bracket's cap. Gains above that may be taxed at 20%.Also, the 0% capital gains bracket applies to federal taxes, but your profits could still be subject to state-level taxes, experts say. Tax planning for the 0% bracketAs income limits rise for the 0% capital gains bracket due to IRS inflation adjustments, more investors could have tax savings opportunities, experts say.   "There is tons of planning to be done here," especially for early retirees with lower income, according to CFP Dinon Hughes, a partner with Nvest Financial in Portsmouth, New Hampshire. One strategy, known as "tax gain harvesting," is selling profitable brokerage account assets during lower-income years to leverage the 0% bracket, he said. Keep in mind, these sales stack on top of your other earnings, which could bump taxable income above the 0% threshold.You can also sell the asset and immediately rebuy it to "reset the cost basis," or original purchase price, said CFP Charles Sachs, chief investment officer of Imperio Wealth Advisors in Coral Gables, Florida.By resetting the cost basis to current market value, you can reduce future capital gains to trim your tax bill.When selling assets at a loss, the "wash sale rule" blocks tax-loss harvesting when you rebuy a "substantially identical" asset within 30 days before or after the sale. But the same rule doesn't apply when harvesting gains.Weigh other tax benefits Managing capital gains is only one part of yearly tax planning, according to Guarino with Baker Newman Noyes. Before selling investments, you should know how boosting AGI could impact your broader financial plan, including income phase-outs for various tax breaks, he said. For example, modified adjusted gross income can impact a range of tax benefits, such as Affordable Care Act health insurance premium subsidies, which can disappear once earnings exceed the federal limits by even a single dollar. Another example is President Donald Trump's temporary $6,000 senior "bonus" deduction, which is worth up to $12,000 for married couples per year through 2028.

schema.headline: How much you can make in 2027 and still pay 0% capital gains tax
